dialogue_quality_notes: Clear, practical proposals (rotation, wash same night, fan/window) with explicit immediate-action requests.
Some needless repetition of the immediate request to turn on the extractor fan across rounds 5–6.
Participants negotiated a concrete schedule and a swap procedure (post in group chat), which is appropriately specific for a speech-only transcript.
Tone is cooperative; agreements are explicit and conditional points are addressed.
evaluation.final_reason: Housemates agreed on concrete shared rules and a stove rotation. Agent A proposed a rotation and cleaning/fan rules (Turn 5: 'Let's try a simple rotation ... Also, everyone wash pans the same night and please turn on the fan and open the window when cooking.'). Agent D accepted the rotation with a swap condition (Turn 6: 'One condition: if someone needs a different night, can we swap with notice?'). Agent A then accepted swaps with notice and posting in the group chat (Turn 7: 'Okay, swaps are fine — just give notice and post the change in the group chat so everyone knows.'), which closed the remaining allocation dispute. The cleaning and fan/window expectations were also mutually stated and accepted.
position_change_notes: Agent A moved from describing current behavior ('I cook most nights and I buy most shared stuff') to accepting a shared rotation and concrete obligations (wash same night, use fan), and later accepted swaps with notice ('Okay, swaps are fine — just give notice and post the change in the group chat').
Agent D moved from complaining about being skipped to requesting a rotation and then accepting the proposed schedule with a swap condition ('One condition: ... swap with notice').
Agents B and C initially raised complaints (smell, unwashed pan) and then accepted the proposed rules (wash same night, turn on fan).
No participant reversed an accepted substantive position after agreement; remaining movement after agreement was limited to requests for immediate action (turn fan on).

round_scores.evidence: Agent A proposed shared rules (clean pans same night, wipe stove, use fan). Agent B accepted and requested immediate action (fan/window) but did not oppose A's proposal—no incompatible demands were expressed.

Agent D introduced a new, incompatible practical demand: a weeknight rotation so D gets stove time ('I get home late and keep getting skipped'). No allocation or schedule had been agreed yet, so a substantive allocation conflict was present and unresolved.

Agent A proposed a concrete rotation (D: Tue/Thu; A: Mon/Wed/Fri) and restated cleaning/fan rules. Agent D accepted but added a condition allowing swaps with notice. The main stove-allocation conflict was largely addressed by the proposed schedule, but the swap procedure/acceptance remained unsettled.

Agent A accepted swaps with notice and posting in the group chat and restated the cleaning and extractor-fan rules: 'Okay, swaps are fine — just give notice and post the change in the group chat so everyone knows.' This produced a concrete, mutually stated arrangement for rotation and swaps, resolving the allocation conflict.
Agent A promised to switch the extractor fan on and open the window now. Agent B reiterated the immediate request but no party opposed the agreement—no substantive conflict present.

Agent C repeated the request for the fan/window and Agent A again promised to switch them on. All parties maintained the previously agreed rules; no new or continuing incompatible demands were expressed.

substantive_insights: Stove-access conflict was primarily about allocation (who cooks when); a simple day-based rotation resolved the core incompatibility.
Cleaning and ventilation concerns were framed as household norms (wash same night, use extractor fan/open window) and accepted without protracted debate.
The swap-with-notice mechanism (and requirement to post changes) addressed practical coordination costs and information asymmetry, turning a contested allocation into a manageable schedule.
